title: ICE Detains Bronx Food Pantry Founder After Court Hearing, and 8,000 Neighbours Lose Their Groceries
excerpt: Aleksander Nilaj, who founded the Open Hand Association pantry on Lydig Avenue, was taken into custody on October 13 and is held at Delaney Hall in New Jersey, while supporters petition ICE to release him.
body:
• Aleksander Nilaj, founder and president of the Open Hand Association food pantry in the Bronx, was taken into ICE custody on October 13 after arriving for a scheduled court hearing, according to a community petition citing the Department of Homeland Security.
  • The pantry on Lydig Avenue serves between 7,000 and 8,000 people a month; staff say they cannot keep up without him and warn it will shut down for good if he does not return.
  • DHS says Nilaj entered the US legally from Albania in 2006, remained past his permitted time and was ordered removed by an immigration judge in 2008.
  • The pantry is currently listed as closed on the Lemontree food-help directory; families who relied on it visited once a week, with registration required and their own bags or cart.

Aleksander Nilaj built a food pantry that feeds thousands of Bronx families every month. On October 13, he arrived for a scheduled court hearing and was taken into custody by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement instead, according to a community petition on Change.org seeking his release. Nilaj is the founder and president of the Open Hand Association Food Pantry on Lydig Avenue. The tracking account Eyes On Ice reported on October 17 that he is being held at the Delaney Hall detention facility in New Jersey.

A pantry that feeds up to 8,000 people a month

Every month, between 7,000 and 8,000 people in the Bronx count on the Open Hand Association pantry for groceries, the petition says. Nilaj has kept it going for 14 years for families who might otherwise go without. A separate humanitarian petition filed in his support puts the figure at approximately 7,500 individuals and families a month and his service at more than 15 years, and says that during the COVID-19 pandemic Nilaj, his wife, his two children and volunteers distributed close to one million meals, reaching neighbouring communities, firehouses, police stations, nursing homes and hospitals.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=G4DHtQuNWJQ

"He made sure that people in need had food on their tables for their families."

— Saimir Burgaj, chairman of the Open Hand Association pantry, speaking to News 12

Staff say they cannot keep up with the work without him, and they have warned the pantry will shut down for good if he does not come back, according to the release petition. The pantry's listing on the Lemontree food-help directory currently marks the Open Hand Association as closed. The listing describes a 501(c)(3) humanitarian nonprofit at 821 Lydig Avenue in the Bronx offering free groceries, fresh produce and, when available, toiletries, diapers and pet food.

What DHS says about his case

The Department of Homeland Security says Nilaj came to the United States legally from Albania in 2006, stayed past his permitted time, and was ordered removed by an immigration judge in 2008, according to the petition's account of the government's position. That history now sits alongside a decade and a half of community service, and the petitions argue the two should be weighed together. Supporters note that he did what the system asks of people in his position: he showed up to court. Arresting someone at a hearing he chose to attend, they argue, tells others that showing up is a risk.

https://x.com/NBCNewYork/status/2112379646482284616

The discretion his supporters are asking for

The petitions do not dispute that ICE has enforcement authority. They ask the agency to use its discretion. The ICE New York City Field Office can release Nilaj while his case is reviewed, and New York's members of Congress can press for a stay of removal, a pause on deportation, so he can return to the pantry, according to the release petition. The humanitarian petition asks reviewing officials to weigh his years of service, the volunteer network he built, and the dependence of thousands of families on the pantry before ordering his removal. For the seniors on fixed incomes, working families living paycheck to paycheck and parents the pantry serves, the petitions argue, losing it means choosing between food and rent, utilities, medication or transport.

What happens next

Nilaj remains in detention at Delaney Hall while supporters press for his release, and the pantry he founded is listed as closed as winter approaches. No decision on a stay of removal or release has been announced. What is already clear is the arithmetic his supporters keep returning to: one man's court date has become a food-supply question for up to 8,000 of his neighbours, and the longer he is held, the harder it becomes for a small volunteer operation built around its founder to reopen at all.
